usage_boundary: Published aggregate facts and public scientific context. No participant-level records, journal figures or inaccessible report contents.

sources.title: Exercise Physiology and Countermeasures
sources.locator: Staying Fit in Microgravity; Key Areas of Research
sources.statement: NASA develops exercise hardware and protocols to address muscle, bone and cardiovascular deconditioning and support mission task performance.
sources.boundary: Education about countermeasures is not an individual exercise prescription.

sources.title: Exercise Overview · OCHMO-TB-031
sources.publisher: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer
sources.statement: NASA connects exercise countermeasures to health maintenance and postflight recovery of aerobic capacity and strength.
sources.boundary: Existing mission prescriptions require qualified oversight. This prototype assigns no intensity, duration or treatment.

sources.title: 4.0 Human Performance
sources.statement: NASA distinguishes aerobic capacity, sensorimotor capabilities and muscular strength within mission health requirements.
sources.boundary: The prototype does not apply these operational standards as individual thresholds or certify fitness for duty.

sources.title: Sensorimotor Risk
sources.statement: Altered gravity can affect postural control, locomotion and fine motor function, particularly around gravity transitions.
sources.boundary: Review an authorised assessment; do not initiate unsupervised standing or balance tests from this app.

sources.title: Aerobic Risk
sources.statement: NASA relates reduced aerobic capacity to task performance and considers the capabilities of exercise countermeasure systems for exploration.
sources.boundary: Neither a heart-rate observation nor recorded plan completion establishes aerobic capacity.

sources.title: Overview of the NASA 70-day Bed Rest Study
sources.statement: The methods overview describes an Earth-based bed-rest campaign and separate pre-, during- and post-bed-rest measurement schedules, including functional and balance assessments.
sources.boundary: This overview does not report study outcomes. Its laboratory schedule is not an astronaut monitoring prescription.

sources.title: Ongoing HRP Research
sources.statement: NASA reports ongoing investigations into how spaceflight affects human health and performance.
sources.boundary: An evolving research programme motivates measurement questions, not individual medical conclusions.

sources.title: Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight
sources.statement: Changing gravity requires adaptation across body systems. Distance from Earth can make immediate medical support harder to obtain.
sources.boundary: A hazard description identifies a relevant question; it does not establish an individual outcome.

sources.title: Risks of Human Spaceflight
sources.statement: NASA identifies changes in circulation and cardiovascular function in weightlessness as a research concern.
sources.boundary: A posture-related HR response is one recorded quantity, not a complete cardiovascular assessment.

sources.title: Risks of Human Spaceflight
sources.locator: Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness
sources.statement: NASA studies how exercise can protect muscular and cardiorespiratory function and support task performance.
sources.boundary: A recorded force change cannot certify overall muscle function, task performance or medical readiness.

sources.title: Risks of Human Spaceflight
sources.locator: Risk of Altered Sensorimotor and Vestibular Function
sources.statement: NASA identifies gait and coordination difficulties during gravity transitions as relevant to walking and operating vehicles.
sources.boundary: A tandem-step observation does not isolate the cause of a change or establish vestibular dysfunction.

sources.title: Risk to Vehicle Crew Egress Capability and Task Performance
sources.statement: NASA treats post-landing egress capability and task performance as a distinct human spaceflight risk.
sources.boundary: The fictional task in this demonstration is not a spacecraft egress assessment.

sources.title: Physiological and Functional Alterations after Spaceflight and Bed Rest
sources.statement: The study included 13 ISS astronauts, 10 bed-rest controls and 9 bed-rest exercisers. It reported associations between physiological and functional changes across session pairs.
sources.boundary: Published associations are contextual, not personal prediction accuracy or a substitute for missing observations. Bed rest is an analog. No individual research records are included.

sources.title: Astronaut Exercise
sources.locator: CEVIS equipment paragraph; VO2max investigation; limitations of transfer
sources.statement: CEVIS controls cycling workload and displays cycling speed, heart rate, elapsed time and prescription details. ARED and T2 support other exercise activities.
sources.boundary: Equipment feasibility does not validate PARALLAX acquisition labels or comparison protocol. No device or NASA medical-system connection is implemented.

sources.title: Hazard: Distance From Earth
sources.locator: Communication delays and greater crew self-reliance
sources.statement: Distance can limit timely Earth support. Local records can help prepare a question for qualified review when connectivity is constrained.
sources.boundary: The local cached demonstration and export are not mission communications, clinical autonomy or successful delivery.

sources.title: In-Flight Medical Reference Page
sources.statement: Established mission procedures and responsible qualified personnel govern assessment and treatment.
sources.boundary: PARALLAX has no validated diagnosis, triage, treatment or emergency-care pathway.

sources.title: Exercise Countermeasures
sources.statement: Documents exercise equipment, physiological monitoring and NASA exercise-data systems. It grounds acquisition context for the fictional cycling example.
sources.boundary: PARALLAX has no connection to these devices or to OnePortal.

sources.title: 6.0 Medical Operations
sources.statement: Establishes the role of mission medical operations and qualified oversight in reviewing crew health.
sources.boundary: PARALLAX does not apply operational medical standards or provide medical authority.

sources.title: 3.0 Health and Medical Care
sources.statement: Places health monitoring within a broader system of crew medical care and responsible personnel.
sources.boundary: The prototype supports evidence review, without diagnosis or treatment.

sources.title: A Clinical Decision Support System for Earth-independent Medical Operations
sources.statement: Explains why deep-space communication delays motivate greater onboard medical capability. PARALLAX explores local evidence review and handoff preparation within this context.
sources.boundary: NASA’s proposed clinical decision support system is a separate research effort. PARALLAX does not implement it.

sources.title: Clinical Decision Support Concept of Operations
sources.statement: Provides research context for clinical decision support during exploration. PARALLAX retains questions for later qualified review.
sources.boundary: Catalogue-level context only; no clinical decision support capability or validated system integration is claimed.
